- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. - fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Review done. The proposal's base (`6271aa75`) is byte-identical to our set across all nine agent-files, so the diff reads cleanly as "what would change for us." It touches four files:

**What it does**

- **prose.md** (the substance): the trailing "Commit description details" paragraph becomes a section, `### Commit titles and descriptions`, with three subsections — the common types, the scope rule, and `#### Project-declared types`. The mechanism: a project may declare a type beyond the common six by naming the type, its scope vocabulary, and its description grammar; declarations live in the project's `custom.md`; a title check admits exactly the common set plus declared names. The set declares one type for itself: `agent-files(<scope>): <to|from> <member-list>, <date>` with scopes `proposal` and `adoption`.
- **AGENTS.md**: retargets `[cdd]` to the new anchor — which also fixes a real pre-existing defect: `[cdd]` and `[cbt]` currently point at the same section, and the sentence citing it is missing its opening paren. Both bugs are in our copy today.
- **rationale.md**: the mirrored why, properly attributed (wink, 2026-08-31).
- **notes.md**: a pure re-wrap of an overlong line. Correction-grade.

**My opinion: adopt it.** The reasoning holds up:

- It changes no behavior rule — it's additive vocabulary, so adoption risk is near zero. It also formalizes something already true: vc-x1's last two commits use the type, so the family's history already contains `agent-files(...)` titles that our current rules technically wouldn't admit.
- Confining declarations to `custom.md` keeps the universal core universal, and explicitly stating that a declared type's scope slot carries the declaration's vocabulary (not a component) confines the one deviation from Conventional-Commit convention instead of letting it leak.

# vc-x1 config file

Configure the work-repo of a dual repo system. The other repo, we call the agent-repo, is
also a markdown configuration file typically named .vc-config.md.

The code blocks in these config files are in toml format and these blocks are logically
concatenated in the order written here and those become the information used for configuring
the system.

The two repos
```toml
[repos]
work = "."
agent = ".claude"
```

The agent-file family this repo belongs to: its member name and the sibling repos it answers to
```toml
[family]
member = "iiac-perf"
template = "../vc-x1-template"
messages = "../vc-x1-messages"
```

The validation commands, each element one invocation, run in order by `vc-x1 validate`
```toml
[validate]
full = [
  "cargo fmt",
  "cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings",
  "cargo test",
  "cargo install --path . --locked",
]
fast = ["cargo test --bins"]
```

1	# Prose and durable text
2	
3	How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
4	commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
5	comments, the cycle-record).
6	
7	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and converges
8	at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)). Project-local
9	content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## Prose form
12	
13	([why](rationale.md#prose-form))
14	
15	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why* or
16	the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
17	[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
18	numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One fact
19	per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they
20	hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their
21	relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See [Semicolons](#semicolons) and [Typeable
22	punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
23	
24	Surfaces that use this shape:
25	
26	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See [Doc
27	  comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
28	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and agent-repo). The title is the commit-specific add-on.
29	  See [The per-rung flow](../AGENTS.md#the-per-rung-flow).
30	- The cycle-record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`. See [The In Progress
31	  block](notes.md#the-in-progress-block).
32	- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are
33	  still fine.
34	
35	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
36	
37	- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, arranged by
38	  [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
39	  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader meets
40	    first and it answers the problem
41	  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them is
42	    a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
43	  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A bullet
44	    wanting a paragraph belongs in the cycle-record instead
45	  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
46	    live in the cycle-record, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names, each
47	    reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs here
48	- **Cycle-record / todo**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what landed
49	  and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list. The diff
50	  is the mechanical record, the commit body the problem and solution, the cycle-record the design
51	  thinking, and none restates another.
52	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
53	
54	### Leads are labels, unmarked
55	
56	In a list item or a numbered step, a lead is a short label ending in a colon, with no markup, and
57	the sentence after it is complete without it:
58	
59	```
60	1. Backfill: fill every as-built ladder whose commits have landed, before anything else.
61	```
62	
63	- Label names, sentence instructs: a reader's eye takes bold at the head of an item as the item's
64	  name and resumes at the plain text expecting a full sentence, so a bold lead that is the
65	  sentence's own verb or subject (`**Backfill** every as-built ladder ...`) loses its imperative to
66	  the reader who skips it. Measured 2026-08-21, at the review of the rule that example is from: the
67	  reviewer read "every as-built ladder" and stopped, with nothing telling them what to do.
68	- The inverted case: a rule stated in bold is the same failure inverted. When the bold is a whole
69	  sentence and the plain text is commentary, the reader who skips bold reads the commentary as the
70	  rule. The fix is the same: a short name as the label, the rule as the plain sentence. The hard
71	  rules in AGENTS.md are the instance, and the names they gained are greppable and survive a
72	  renumbering.
73	- Definitions: the same shape, `Term: what it means.` A period after a bold term (`**Term.** ...`)
74	  reads as a heading, which is the label reading again.
75	- No markup on the label: bold is what makes the eye treat the lead as a heading and skip it, and
76	  the agent-files are read by an agent, which needs no emphasis. The colon alone marks the label
77	  (wink, 2026-08-21).
78	- The price: one word of redundancy, paid on purpose: the label is skippable, the sentence is not.
79	
80	### One spelling per term
81	
82	A defined term has one spelling, everywhere: `work-repo` and `agent-repo` are always hyphenated,
83	`agent-files`, `version-of-record`, `dual-repo`, and `as-built` likewise, and no rule varies the
84	spelling by how the term is used. Terminology in AGENTS.md defines the terms, and this section is
85	where the spelling rule lives, since a glossary is read for meaning rather than for spelling.
86	
87	### Bullet form
88	
89	A bullet is a full sentence, capitalized and ending in a period or question mark, unless the list
90	is a plain list of things (files, names, options), which takes neither. A list is all one or all
91	the other. A sentence never opens with a lower-case name (`squash-push`, `rationale.md`), it is

93	
94	### Line widths
95	
96	Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather than

99	
100	- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
101	- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default

103	- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
104	- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
105	  convention here 2026-08-09, and published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.
106	
107	The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps when
108	touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than imitating the
109	narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL, a literal report
110	row, indented code in a comment).
111	
112	### Problem-first shape
113	
114	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper form of the same

116	
117	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate what
118	  follows it.
119	- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms, answering

# Commit model

Two commit bodies from the `config loader` cycle in [cycle-model.md](cycle-model.md), shown as
specimens rather than a skeleton: a work rung's body and a bookend's. Copy the shape, not the
words. The rules are in [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form).

## A work rung

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with
    its path, so a caller that only wants to know which file was read
    stops there.
  - `config::parser` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands
    it a string and never touches the filesystem.
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field
    access moves behind the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows
    the file's shape.
```

The intro states this commit's problem and defines "split", the word the title assumes. Each `*`
is one facet of it, each `-` under a `*` answers that facet, and nothing names a file that the
diff already lists.

A bookend resolves no problem of its own, so its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the
